title: SHAP for usage features
prompt: Your churn GBM includes `seats`, `active_users_30d`, and `warehouses`, which correlate at 0.85+ with each other. Mean |SHAP| for `seats` is nearly zero; `active_users_30d` is the top feature.
ai: SHAP is a principled, game-theoretic attribution, so a near-zero mean |SHAP| means `seats` has essentially **no relationship with churn**. We can tell the account team that seat count doesn't matter for retention.
why: With correlated features the model can route the signal through one of them; low SHAP means the model didn't use seats, not that seats is unrelated to churn
flaws: Correlated features soak up seats' credit
SHAP values must be normalized to compare
Mean SHAP, not mean |SHAP|, shows relevance
TreeSHAP is only exact for depth ≤ 3 trees
model: SHAP explains the model's choices, not the world. If two features carry the same signal, the model may pick one and ignore the other.
mech: Trees split on whichever correlated feature looks slightly better at each node. Once `active_users_30d` captures the size signal, `seats` adds little, so its attributions shrink. Retrain without `active_users_30d` and `seats` would likely light up.
breaks: Low importance means 'not needed given the other features', not 'irrelevant'. And even high SHAP isn't causal.
contrast: 'Given active users and warehouses, seats adds little predictive information' is a fair statement.
details: Check the marginal relationship (churn rate by seat decile), group correlated features and attribute to the group, or compare model performance with and without the group.
fix: Group the size features (seats, active users, warehouses) and report their combined importance; show churn by seat decile for the account team.

title: What a monotone constraint guarantees
prompt: You set `monotone_constraints` so predicted churn can only decrease as `support_tickets_resolved` increases. What does that guarantee?
ai: It guarantees that for any fixed values of the other features, increasing `support_tickets_resolved` never increases the prediction. It does **not** mean the overall (marginal) relationship in the data is monotone, and it isn't a causal claim. It works by rejecting splits that would put a higher leaf value on the larger side and by bounding descendant leaf values. It often costs a bit of fit but improves extrapolation and trust.
why: Accurate: ceteris-paribus monotonicity in the model, enforced at split/leaf level, not causal
model: It's a guard rail on the model's surface along one axis, holding everything else still.
mech: During tree building, a split on the constrained feature is only allowed if the child on the higher side gets a leaf value no larger than the lower side, and child values are bounded so deeper splits can't violate it. Summed over trees, the whole prediction stays monotone.
breaks: If the true relationship is non-monotone, the constraint forces bias. It also says nothing about what happens if you intervene on the feature in the real world.
contrast: A PDP that slopes down is a weaker property (average over other features), and can hide non-monotone slices.
details: LightGBM offers `monotone_constraints_method` = basic, intermediate, or advanced, trading strictness for fit.

title: 80% prediction intervals
prompt: You need 80% prediction intervals for monthly credits. You train two LightGBMs with `objective='quantile'`, alpha = 0.1 and 0.9.
ai: Each model minimizes the pinball loss at its alpha, so it learns the conditional 10th and 90th percentiles. The interval [q10, q90] therefore has **guaranteed 80% coverage** on new data.
why: Quantile GBMs approximate quantiles; nothing guarantees coverage (and the two curves can even cross)
flaws: Quantile models don't guarantee coverage
Pinball loss estimates the mean, not quantiles
Alphas should be 0.2 and 0.8 for an 80% band
Quantile objectives need a log link here
model: A model aimed at the 90th percentile is an estimate of it, not a promise. Coverage is something you check, not something you get for free.
mech: With finite data, regularization, and early stopping, the learned quantiles are biased and noisy, especially in sparse regions. The two models are trained independently, so q10 can exceed q90 for some rows. Real coverage is often well below 80%.
breaks: Check empirical coverage on held-out data, and fix it with conformalized quantile regression (CQR), which widens the intervals by a calibrated amount.
contrast: The pinball-loss part is right: minimizing it at α targets the α-quantile.
details: CQR: on a calibration set compute $E_i = \max(q_{lo}(x_i) - y_i,\; y_i - q_{hi}(x_i))$, take the $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$-th smallest value $\hat Q$, and report $[q_{lo}-\hat Q,\; q_{hi}+\hat Q]$. That gives finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability.
fix: Fit q10/q90, then conformalize on a held-out calibration set (CQR) and verify coverage by segment.
bug: Quantile GBMs approximate quantiles; nothing guarantees coverage (and the two curves can even cross)

title: Tweedie model predictions
prompt: Monthly credits are zero for many accounts and long-tailed otherwise. You train LightGBM with `objective='tweedie'`, `tweedie_variance_power=1.5`.
ai:
Good objective choice for zero-inflated, positive data. Tweedie uses a log link, so the raw predictions are on the log scale:

```python
pred_credits = np.exp(model.predict(X_new))
```
why: LightGBM's predict() already returns the response scale for tweedie; exponentiating again blows up predictions
flaws: predict() already applies the inverse link
Variance power must be exactly 1 or 2 here
Tweedie loss can't handle exact zeros in y
Should train RMSE on log1p(credits) instead
model: Know which side of the link function you're on. The model's score lives on the log scale; predict() hands you dollars, not logs.
mech: Internally the trees add up a log-mean score. LightGBM's predict() applies exp() for log-link objectives (poisson, gamma, tweedie) unless you ask for `raw_score=True`. Calling exp() again turns a prediction of 100 into e^100.
breaks: If you call `predict(X, raw_score=True)` you do get the log-scale score, and then exp() is right.
contrast: Choosing Tweedie with power between 1 and 2 for zero-heavy positive data is correct.
details: Tweedie with $1<p<2$ is a compound Poisson–gamma: a point mass at zero plus a continuous positive part, with $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\phi\mu^p$.
fix:
```python
pred_credits = model.predict(X_new)            # already on credits scale
# or: np.exp(model.predict(X_new, raw_score=True))
```

title: What max_bin does
prompt: Explain LightGBM's `max_bin` and when you'd change it.
ai: LightGBM pre-buckets each continuous feature into at most `max_bin` histogram bins (default 255), and splits are only considered at bin boundaries. That's a big part of why it's fast and memory-light. Lowering it speeds training and acts as mild regularization; raising it allows finer splits, which can help on large datasets with features where precise thresholds matter, but can overfit on small data.
why: Accurate description of histogram binning and its trade-offs
model: Instead of checking every possible cut point, round the ruler to 255 marks and only cut on the marks.
mech: Gradients and Hessians are summed per bin once, then the best split is found by scanning bins, not sorted values. Fewer bins = faster scans and coarser thresholds.
breaks: If a feature has a meaningful threshold between two bin edges (e.g., an exact pricing tier), coarse bins can blur it.
contrast: XGBoost's `tree_method='hist'` uses the same idea, with `max_bin` defaulting to 256.
details: Bins are built from quantiles of a sample of the data (`bin_construct_sample_cnt`).

title: Encoding a missing recency feature
prompt: Your feature `days_since_last_query` is missing for accounts that never queried. A colleague fills NaN with -999 before XGBoost.
ai: That's harmless. Trees only care about order, and -999 sits below every real value, so the model can isolate missing rows with one split. It's equivalent to leaving NaN in, since XGBoost's native handling also just sends missing rows to one side.
why: Not equivalent: native NaN handling learns the best side at every split; -999 is always forced to the low side
flaws: NaN routing is learned; -999 is stuck low
Trees can't split on negative feature values
-999 distorts the loss gradient for those rows
XGBoost needs NaN imputed with the median
model: NaN gets a free pass to whichever branch helps. -999 is stuck at the left end of the ruler.
mech: At each split XGBoost tries sending missing rows left and right and keeps the better one. With -999, missing rows always go wherever 'very small' values go. If missing behaves like 'very large' (never queried ≈ infinite days since), the model needs extra splits to carve them out, wasting depth.
breaks: The sentinel is close to harmless with deep trees and plenty of data, and it's fine when missing really does behave like the smallest values. It's also a problem for linear boosters and for monotone constraints.
contrast: Saying a sentinel is 'usually workable' is fair. Saying it's 'equivalent' isn't.
details: Here the natural encoding is a large value (or NaN plus an `ever_queried` flag), since never querying is the extreme of 'long time since last query'.
fix: Leave NaN for XGBoost to route, and add `ever_queried` as an explicit flag if it carries meaning.
bug: Not equivalent: native NaN handling learns the best side at every split; -999 is always forced to the low side

title: Permutation importance on validation
prompt: You compute permutation importance on the validation set for a GBM where `credits_last_30d` and `credits_last_90d` correlate at 0.95.
ai: Permutation importance on held-out data is model-agnostic and unbiased, so unlike gain importance it handles correlated features correctly. Both credit features show low importance, so neither matters much.
why: Correlated features mask each other in permutation importance, and permuting one creates unrealistic rows
flaws: Correlated twins mask each other's importance
Permutation importance needs training data
Permutation is only valid for linear models
You should permute the target, not features
model: If you hide one of two identical keys, the door still opens. Neither key looks important.
mech: Shuffling `credits_last_30d` breaks it, but the model can still lean on `credits_last_90d`, so the loss barely rises. The same happens in reverse. Also, the shuffled rows pair a high 30-day value with a low 90-day value, combinations that never occur, so the model is probed off its data.
breaks: Permute correlated features together as a group (or use conditional permutation). Then the pair's importance shows up.
contrast: It's true that permutation importance on held-out data avoids gain importance's bias toward high-cardinality features.
details: Grouped permutation importance: shuffle the rows of a block of columns jointly, keeping their within-row relationship.
fix: Cluster features by correlation, permute each cluster jointly, and report cluster-level importance.
bug: Correlated features mask each other in permutation importance, and permuting one creates unrealistic rows

title: Number of rounds after CV
prompt: You ran `lgb.cv` with 5 folds and early stopping; the best mean CV score was at 840 rounds. How do you train the final model?
ai: Retrain on all the training data with `num_boost_round=840` and no early stopping (there's no validation set left to watch). Some people scale it up slightly, say by 1/(1 − 1/k) ≈ 1.25 for 5 folds, because the full set is 25% larger than each training fold; either is defensible. Keep the test set untouched for the final estimate.
why: Standard, valid practice for choosing rounds after CV
model: CV tells you how long to cook; the final dish uses all the ingredients for about that long.
mech: The best iteration is a property of the learning rate and data size. With all the data, the optimum is similar or slightly later, so 840 (or a bit more) is a good choice.
breaks: If data has a time structure, use the time-respecting CV's rounds and retrain on data up to the cutoff.
contrast: Early stopping on the test set to pick rounds would make the test estimate optimistic.
details: The best number of rounds tends to grow slowly with n, which is the rationale for the modest scale-up.

title: Calibrated probabilities at 1% positives
prompt: Positives are 1%. You need calibrated probabilities to compute expected cost per account.
ai: Train with `scale_pos_weight` (or `is_unbalance`) if it helps ranking, but know it inflates predicted probabilities, since the model is fitting a reweighted world. Then recalibrate on a held-out calibration set that has the true 1% prevalence, using isotonic regression if you have plenty of positives or Platt scaling if not. Check with a reliability curve and Brier score.
why: Reweighting distorts probabilities; recalibrating on held-out data at true prevalence fixes it
model: Reweighting changes the world the model believes it lives in. Calibration moves it back to the real one.
mech: Upweighting positives makes them look common, so scores shift up. Calibration learns a monotone map from scores to observed frequencies in real-prevalence data, preserving ranking while fixing the levels.
breaks: Isotonic overfits with few positives (step artifacts). Calibrating on training data or a rebalanced set doesn't fix anything.
contrast: Without reweighting, a well-regularized GBM with log loss is often reasonably calibrated already, and you may not need it at all.
details: Prior correction alternative: with weight w on positives, $\text{odds}_{true} \approx \text{odds}_{model}/w$.

title: lambda vs gamma in XGBoost
prompt: Explain XGBoost's `lambda` and `gamma` regularization.
ai: `lambda` is the minimum loss reduction required to make a split: higher lambda means fewer splits. `gamma` is the L2 penalty on leaf weights, shrinking each leaf toward zero as $w^* = -\frac{G}{H+\gamma}$.
why: The two are swapped: gamma is the split threshold, lambda is the L2 penalty on leaf weights
flaws: lambda and gamma definitions are swapped
Optimal leaf weight is −G/H, unregularized
lambda is the L1 penalty, not an L2 one
gamma applies only at the tree's root split
model: Gamma is the toll to build a new branch. Lambda is the brake on how far any leaf can move its prediction.
mech: Lambda sits in the denominator of the leaf weight, $-G/(H+\lambda)$, pulling leaves with little Hessian mass toward zero. Gamma is subtracted from the split gain, so a split must improve loss by more than gamma to be kept.
breaks: Both regularize but act differently: gamma prunes structure, lambda shrinks values. `alpha` is the L1 penalty on leaf weights.
contrast: The leaf-weight formula form is right; only the symbol is wrong.
details: $$\text{Gain} = \tfrac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right] - \gamma$$
fix: `gamma` (min_split_loss): minimum gain to split. `lambda` (reg_lambda): L2 on leaf weights, $w^*=-G/(H+\lambda)$.
bug: The two are swapped: gamma is the split threshold, lambda is the L2 penalty on leaf weights

title: Reading a PDP for seats
prompt: Your credits model uses `seats` and `warehouses` (correlation 0.8). The PDP for `seats` rises steeply from 10 to 500. A PM asks what happens if a 20-warehouse account adds seats.

flaws: PDP averages over impossible combinations
PDPs are only meaningful for linear models
Gain importance should answer this instead
PDP must be computed on training data only

mech: To draw the curve, the PDP sets seats to 400 for every row while keeping each row's warehouses, creating 400-seat, 1-warehouse accounts the model never saw. The curve mixes in-distribution and off-distribution predictions and averages over all accounts, not this one.
breaks: ALE plots use only local, realistic changes; ICE curves show the individual account's line. Neither turns a predictive model into a causal one.
contrast: 'On average, the model predicts more credits for accounts with more seats' is a fair reading of the PDP.
details: PDP: $\hat f_S(x_s) = \frac1n\sum_i \hat f(x_s, x_{C,i})$. ALE integrates local derivatives within conditional slices of $x_s$.

title: October churn feature query
prompt:

```sql
SELECT a.account_id,
       SUM(c.credits) AS credits_last_30d
FROM accounts a
JOIN credit_usage c ON c.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE c.usage_date >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY 1;
```
ai: The 30-day credit window is a strong, well-built feature: it's a recent, aggregated usage signal, and the GBM can learn nonlinear thresholds in it. Training AUC 0.95 and validation AUC 0.94 confirm it generalizes.
why: The window is anchored on CURRENT_DATE, not the scoring date, so it includes October usage (the label period)
flaws: Feature window runs past the scoring date
SUM should be AVG for a 30-day usage window
Close train/val AUC proves there's no leakage
GROUP BY 1 groups on credits, not account

breaks: Training and validation scores agreeing never rules out leakage when both are built the same way. A forward-time backtest built with point-in-time joins would expose it.

```sql
       COALESCE(SUM(c.credits), 0) AS credits_last_30d
FROM accounts a
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DATE '2026-09-30' AS as_of_date) s
LEFT JOIN credit_usage c
  ON c.account_id = a.account_id
 AND c.usage_date BETWEEN DATEADD(day, -29, s.as_of_date) AND s.as_of_date
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

title: Matching on pre-period credits
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. You matched on the **6-month average** of pre-adoption credits. Standardized mean differences on it are 0.01, and KS p-values look fine.
ai: Balance is excellent: SMD of 0.01 is far below the 0.1 rule of thumb and the KS test shows the distributions match. Matched controls are a valid counterfactual for adopters, so the post-period gap is the effect.
why: Matching on a 6-month average can hide very different trends; adopters are growing and controls are flat
flaws: Matched on the level, not the pre-trend
SMD of 0.01 is so low it signals overfitting
KS tests aren't valid on matched samples
Should also match on post-period credits
model: Two cars can have the same average speed over the last hour while one is accelerating and the other is braking. Where they'll be next depends on the trajectory.
mech: Adopters tend to be accounts that were ramping up. Matching on the average pairs them with steady accounts of the same average. After adoption, adopters keep climbing because of their pre-existing momentum, and the gap gets credited to CodePilot.
breaks: Balance must be checked on what predicts the untreated future outcome. For credits that's the recent lags individually (t−1, t−2, t−3...) or the trend, not just one summary.
contrast: If both groups had flat, matching trajectories, balancing the average would be enough.
details: Include several lags (or level plus slope) in the GenMatch covariate set and check balance on each, then plot treated vs matched-control mean credits by month relative to adoption.
fix: Match on monthly lags t−1…t−6 (or level + slope), re-check balance per lag, and show the event-time plot before claiming an effect.
bug: Matching on a 6-month average can hide very different trends; adopters are growing and controls are flat

title: Choosing the matching window
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. Most accounts run a 30-day CodePilot **trial** before formally adopting, and trial usage drives extra warehouse queries. You match on credits in month t−1 (the month before formal adoption).
ai: Using t−1 credits is the strongest choice: the most recent lag is the best predictor of the counterfactual, and it's pre-treatment by definition because adoption happens at t.
why: Month t−1 is the trial month, already affected by the treatment (anticipation); the true start is the trial
flaws: Month t−1 is the trial, so it's affected
Should match on t+1 to capture the ramp-up
Older lags predict better than recent ones
t−1 credits need log scaling before matching
model: 'Pre-treatment' means before anything changed, not before the paperwork. Date the treatment from when it can first affect behavior.
mech: During the trial, adopters already use CodePilot, so t−1 credits are inflated. Matching them to controls with equally high t−1 credits (who got there naturally) erases the trial's boost from the comparison, and with regression to the mean the post-period gap can shrink or flip.
breaks: Redefine the treatment date as trial start, match on lags before it (t−2 and earlier relative to adoption), and show the event-time plot so any anticipation dip or bump is visible.
contrast: If there were no trial and no anticipation, the most recent lag would indeed be the best single covariate.
details: This is the 'no anticipation' assumption. With it violated, the comparison estimates the effect from t onward net of what already happened in the trial.
fix: Treatment date = trial start. Match on credits from months before the trial; report effects in event time from the trial month.
bug: Month t−1 is the trial month, already affected by the treatment (anticipation); the true start is the trial

title: Six-month outcome sample
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. To 'clean' the data, the analysis keeps only accounts **still active 6 months after the adoption date** (for controls, 6 months after their matched date). Accounts that went dormant are dropped.
ai: Restricting to accounts active at 6 months is sensible. Dormant accounts add noise with near-zero credits, and since we apply the same rule to both groups, it can't introduce bias.
why: Survival is affected by both adoption and credit trajectory, so conditioning on it is collider/selection bias
flaws: Filtering on survival conditions on a collider
Six months is too short a survival window
The active-only filter mainly inflates the SE
Near-zero credits should be log-transformed
model: Applying the same filter to both groups is fair only if the filter is decided before treatment. A filter decided by the outcome race tilts the race.
mech: If CodePilot keeps marginal accounts alive, the adopter survivors include weaker, lower-credit accounts that would have gone dormant, while control survivors are only the strong ones. The comparison is then between different kinds of accounts, biasing the effect (here, toward zero or negative).
breaks: Keep everyone and model dormancy as part of the outcome (credits = 0), or estimate effects on survival separately. Principal stratification is the formal tool for 'effect among those who would survive either way'.
contrast: Dropping accounts based on pre-adoption activity (e.g., dormant before the matching date) is fine.
details: Survival S is caused by D (adoption) and by U (underlying account health), which also drives Y. Conditioning on S opens D → S ← U → Y.
fix: Keep all matched accounts; treat dormancy as credits = 0, and report the effect on dormancy separately.
bug: Survival is affected by both adoption and credit trajectory, so conditioning on it is collider/selection bias

title: Staggered DiD estimator choice
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. Adoption is staggered from January to September 2026. What estimator would you use for a DiD-style analysis, and what does it assume?
ai: Estimate group-time ATTs (Callaway & Sant'Anna): for each adoption cohort g and month t, compare the cohort's change from g−1 to t against accounts **not yet treated** by t (or never treated). Aggregate into an event-study curve and an overall ATT. This avoids TWFE's problem of using already-treated accounts as controls. It assumes parallel trends between each cohort and its comparison group (optionally conditional on covariates) and no anticipation, and it estimates the ATT, not the effect for non-adopters.
why: Correct estimator, assumptions, and estimand for staggered adoption
model: Compare each wave of adopters only with accounts that haven't jumped yet, then stitch the comparisons together.
mech: Every comparison is a clean 2×2 DiD: a cohort before vs after, against units untouched in that window. Heterogeneous or growing effects can't leak in through already-treated controls.
breaks: Late in the panel, few not-yet-treated accounts remain, so estimates get noisy. If late adopters differ from early ones (e.g., in growth), parallel trends can fail.
contrast: A single TWFE regression with an adoption dummy would weight comparisons oddly and can even flip sign with dynamic effects.
details: $ATT(g,t) = E[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid G=g] - E[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid \text{not yet treated at } t]$, with optional doubly robust covariate adjustment.

title: Sample size after matching
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. 1,200 adopters are matched 1:1 **with replacement** to controls. Only 310 distinct controls were used; a few were reused 40+ times.
ai: We have 1,200 matched pairs, so n = 2,400. A two-sample t-test on post-period credits gives SE = 38 and the effect is highly significant.
why: Reused controls are not independent observations; the t-test overstates precision and heavy reuse makes the estimate fragile
flaws: Reused controls overstate the effective n
Matching with replacement is always biased
A paired t-test on the 1,200 pairs fixes it
Bootstrapping the matches is the standard fix
model: Counting the same witness 40 times doesn't give you 40 testimonies.
mech: Each reused control's noise enters the estimate many times, so its variance counts for more. Treating 1,200 control slots as 1,200 independent draws understates the SE. With one control used 40 times, its quirks drive a big slice of the result.
breaks: Report the effective sample size of the control weights, cap reuse or add a caliper, and use Abadie–Imbens standard errors (the naive bootstrap is also invalid here).
contrast: Matching with replacement is a fine choice for reducing bias. The problem is only the inference.
details: With control weights $w_j$ (times used), effective $n_{ctrl} = (\sum w_j)^2/\sum w_j^2$. With heavy reuse that can be 100 or fewer.
fix: Weighted analysis with Abadie–Imbens SEs, report effective n, and check sensitivity when capping reuse at, e.g., 5.
bug: Reused controls are not independent observations; the t-test overstates precision and heavy reuse makes the estimate fragile

title: Accounts within one org
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. Large customers have several accounts under one org. When one team's account adopts CodePilot, it often shares generated pipelines with sibling accounts. Many matched controls are siblings of adopters.
ai: Spillover means the treatment's effects spread beyond adopters, so our estimate captures that broader impact. If anything, it makes the effect look **bigger** than the direct effect, so treat it as an upper bound.
why: Spillover onto control siblings raises control credits, biasing the adopter-vs-control gap toward zero
flaws: Spillover onto controls shrinks the gap
SUTVA concerns only outcome measurement error
Siblings' credits should count as adopters'
Spillover biases the SE, not the estimate
model: If the medicine also helps the people in the next bed, the treated-vs-untreated gap understates what the medicine does.
mech: Sibling controls get extra pipelines and queries from the adopter's work, so their credits rise too. The comparison subtracts some of the effect from itself.
breaks: Match on controls from orgs with no adopters (or analyze at the org level), and measure the spillover separately by comparing sibling accounts with similar accounts in non-adopting orgs.
contrast: If spillover reached only other adopters, it would make the measured effect larger.
details: SUTVA requires a unit's outcome to depend only on its own treatment. Here $Y_j$ for a control depends on $D_i$ of a sibling.
fix: Restrict controls to orgs with no adopters, or cluster/aggregate at the org level, and report the spillover effect on siblings.
bug: Spillover onto control siblings raises control credits, biasing the adopter-vs-control gap toward zero

title: Parallel trends: levels or logs?
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. Adopters average 4,000 credits/month pre-adoption, controls 1,000. Pre-period event-study in **levels** looks flat (parallel). You plan to report the effect as a percentage using log credits.
ai: Parallel trends held in the pre-period, so we're good. Switching to log credits for the DiD is just a rescaling for interpretability; parallel trends carries over to logs automatically.
why: Parallel trends is scale-dependent: parallel in levels with different baselines implies non-parallel in logs
flaws: Parallel trends doesn't carry over to logs
Log outcomes can't be used in a DiD model
Flat pre-trends prove parallel trends hold
A 4× baseline gap rules out DiD entirely
model: If both grow by +100 credits a month, the small account grows 10% and the big one 2.5%. Same steps, different percentages.
mech: Parallel trends is an assumption about the untreated changes on a particular scale. With a 4× baseline gap, equal additive trends become unequal percentage trends, so the log DiD picks up a spurious difference.
breaks: Choose the scale where the assumption is credible (often logs when growth is multiplicative), check pre-trends on that scale, or use Poisson regression / a ratio-of-means estimand.
contrast: If both groups had similar baselines, levels and logs would roughly agree.
details: If $E[\Delta Y(0)]$ is equal across groups in levels, then $\Delta \log Y(0) \approx \Delta Y(0)/Y$ differs by the baseline ratio.
fix: Re-run the event study in logs (or Poisson) and check pre-trends there; report both scales if they disagree.
bug: Parallel trends is scale-dependent: parallel in levels with different baselines implies non-parallel in logs

title: What GenMatch optimizes
prompt: Explain what GenMatch does differently from Mahalanobis or propensity score matching.
ai: GenMatch (Diamond & Sekhon) generalizes Mahalanobis distance by adding a weight for each covariate (the propensity score can be one of them). A genetic algorithm searches over those weights, and for each candidate it runs the matching and measures balance. By default it maximizes the **smallest p-value** across balance tests (paired t-tests and KS tests) on the covariates, so it targets the worst-balanced covariate. It never looks at the outcome. Results depend on the covariates and balance metric you specify, and it doesn't address unobserved confounding.
why: Accurate description of GenMatch's weighted distance, genetic search, and default loss
model: Instead of fixing how much each covariate matters, let a search tune the knobs until the worst-balanced covariate looks as good as possible.
mech: Each candidate weight vector defines a distance, a matched set, and a balance report. The genetic algorithm keeps the weight vectors with the best worst-case balance and breeds new candidates from them.
breaks: Maximizing p-values depends on n; you can also use standardized differences or QQ-based losses. Balance on observed covariates says nothing about unobserved ones.
contrast: Propensity score matching balances covariates only in expectation via one scalar; GenMatch checks balance directly in the matched sample.
details: Distance $d(X_i,X_j) = \sqrt{(X_i-X_j)^\top (S^{-1/2})^\top W S^{-1/2}(X_i-X_j)}$, with W a diagonal weight matrix found by the search.

title: LDV vs DiD disagree
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. A lagged-dependent-variable regression (control for pre-period credits) gives +180 credits/month. A DiD gives +260. What do you make of it?
ai: That's expected. The two rely on different assumptions: LDV assumes selection on the past outcome (unconfoundedness given lags), DiD assumes parallel trends with a fixed unobserved difference. Under common conditions they **bracket** the true effect: if DiD is right, LDV tends to understate a positive effect; if LDV is right, DiD tends to overstate it. So +180 to +260 is a reasonable range, and you should show both rather than pick the one you like.
why: Correct use of the Angrist–Pischke bracketing property
model: Two flashlights from different angles. If they're aimed at different assumptions, the truth usually sits between their beams.
mech: If adopters have a persistent high level (fixed effect), LDV under-adjusts and DiD is right. If adopters had a temporary spike that would fade, DiD over-adjusts and LDV is right. Each one's bias goes in the opposite direction from the other's.
breaks: The bracketing result needs assumptions about the dynamics (e.g., stationarity of the outcome process); with strong trends both can be off in the same direction.
contrast: Saying 'they should agree, so one must have a bug' would be the wrong reading.
details: Angrist & Pischke (Mostly Harmless Econometrics, §5.4): with a positive effect, LDV estimates are a lower bound and FE/DiD an upper bound under their respective models.

title: From ATT to a rollout forecast
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. The matched estimate is ATT = +220 credits/month per adopter (95% CI 150 to 290). 7,800 accounts haven't adopted.
ai: The ATT is the average effect of adoption, so if sales gets the remaining 7,800 accounts to adopt, expect about 7,800 × 220 ≈ **1.7M extra credits/month**.
why: ATT applies to the kind of accounts that chose to adopt; non-adopters (ATU) likely gain less
flaws: ATT doesn't transfer to non-adopters (ATU)
The CI should shrink by √7,800 when scaled
ATT only describes the matched controls
Effects can't be multiplied by account counts
model: People who sign up for the gym first are the ones who'll use it most. Their results don't transfer to the reluctant.
mech: Adopters are engineering-heavy, growing accounts with lots of code to write, exactly where an AI coding assistant pays off. Matching makes the comparison fair for them, but says nothing about accounts with little coding work. Pushed adoption also tends to mean lighter use.
breaks: To forecast, model effect heterogeneity on covariates and reweight to non-adopters' profile (estimating the ATU), and only within common support; ideally validate with a randomized nudge.
contrast: 'Adopters gained about 220 credits/month on average' is exactly what the ATT supports.
details: ATE = π·ATT + (1−π)·ATU. With selection on gains, ATU < ATT.
fix: Estimate CATEs by account profile, reweight to the non-adopter mix (ATU), and report a range; consider a randomized encouragement test.
bug: ATT applies to the kind of accounts that chose to adopt; non-adopters (ATU) likely gain less

title: Reading Γ = 1.8
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. A Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis on the matched pairs says the result stays significant up to **Γ = 1.8**.
ai: It means that if an unobserved confounder made one account in a matched pair up to 1.8 times as likely (in odds) to adopt as its match, the conclusion of a positive effect would still hold at the 5% level. Beyond 1.8, it could be explained away. Whether 1.8 is reassuring depends on context: compare it with how much the strongest observed covariates shift adoption odds.
why: Correct interpretation of Γ as the hidden-bias odds ratio the result can tolerate
model: Γ is how crooked the coin flip inside each pair can be before your finding could be a fluke of hidden bias.
mech: In a perfectly matched pair, each account should be equally likely to have adopted (odds 1). Γ bounds how far hidden differences could push that, and the test asks whether the result survives the worst case at that bound.
breaks: Γ isn't the effect size, and a high Γ isn't proof; it only says how strong unobserved bias would need to be.
contrast: 'Γ = 1.8 means the effect is 1.8× larger than the bias' is a common misreading.
details: Within pair, $\frac{1}{\Gamma} \le \frac{\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)}{\pi_j/(1-\pi_j)} \le \Gamma$.

title: Placebo test result
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. You rerun the full pipeline with a fake adoption date 6 months earlier for every adopter. The placebo effect is +4 credits (CI −30 to +38).
ai: The placebo is null, which shows matched controls and adopters weren't diverging before adoption. That rules out unobserved confounding, so the main estimate is unbiased.
why: A null placebo supports pre-period comparability but can't rule out confounders that change at the same time as adoption
flaws: Can't detect shocks timed with adoption
Placebo window should come after adoption
A null placebo means the true effect is zero
Placebo tests only work with randomized data
model: A placebo is a smoke detector for things that were already burning. It can't hear a fire that starts the same day.
mech: If accounts adopt CodePilot because they're kicking off a big new data platform build, credits jump for that reason too, starting at adoption. There's no divergence 6 months earlier, so the placebo passes while the estimate still includes the project's credits.
breaks: Combine with negative-control outcomes, sensitivity analysis (Γ or E-values), and if possible measures of concurrent events (new warehouses, hiring).
contrast: 'The placebo supports no pre-existing divergence' is a fair conclusion.
details: Placebo-in-time tests the identifying assumption over a window where the effect is known to be zero; it's informative about time-stable confounding, not time-varying shocks at adoption.
fix: Report the placebo as supportive, then add sensitivity analysis and checks on concurrent changes (e.g., new warehouses created in the adoption month).
bug: A null placebo supports pre-period comparability but can't rule out confounders that change at the same time as adoption

title: Clustering standard errors
prompt: **Setup:** Nimbus Cloud (fictional) launched *CodePilot*, an AI coding assistant. Accounts adopt at different times. You estimate the effect of adoption on monthly compute credits using matched controls (GenMatch) on lagged credits and firmographics, then compare post-adoption credits. CodePilot is turned on by an **org admin**, so all accounts in an org adopt together. You have 9,000 accounts in 1,400 orgs and a monthly panel.
ai: Use cluster-robust standard errors clustered by **account**, since we observe each account repeatedly and its months are correlated. That gives SE = 21 and a tight CI.
why: Treatment is assigned at the org level, so errors must be clustered by org; account clustering overstates precision
flaws: Cluster by org, where treatment is assigned
Should cluster by month to handle shocks
Clustering is unnecessary after matching
HC1 robust SEs are enough without clusters
model: You have as many independent experiments as independent decisions. Here, the org admin made the decision.
mech: Accounts in an org share the adoption decision and many shocks (budgets, migrations). Their outcomes move together, so they're not independent pieces of evidence. With ~1,400 orgs (and fewer adopting ones), the true SE is larger.
breaks: Clustering at the assignment level is the safe default (Abadie et al. 2023). With few clusters (< 30–50 treated), use wild cluster bootstrap.
contrast: If adoption were decided account by account with no shared shocks, account-level clustering would be right.
details: Ignoring within-org correlation ρ inflates precision by roughly the design effect 1 + (m−1)ρ, where m is accounts per org.
fix: Cluster by org (and check with a wild cluster bootstrap); consider analyzing at the org level.
bug: Treatment is assigned at the org level, so errors must be clustered by org; account clustering overstates precision

title: Consolidating activity intervals
prompt: In PostgreSQL, merge each account's overlapping or touching intervals into maximal intervals. Endpoints are non-null integers with start_min < end_min; interval_id is unique. Judge the query for arbitrary valid inputs.
fix:
WITH prior AS (
  SELECT *, MAX(end_min) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY start_min, interval_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
  ) AS prior_end
  FROM sessions
), marked AS (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN prior_end IS NULL OR start_min > prior_end
                 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_group
  FROM prior
), grouped AS (
  SELECT *, SUM(new_group) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY start_min, interval_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS grp
  FROM marked
)
SELECT account_id, MIN(start_min) AS start_min, MAX(end_min) AS end_min
FROM grouped
GROUP BY account_id, grp
ORDER BY account_id, start_min;
model: Keep the farthest boundary reached, rather than the endpoint of the last interval you read.
mech: A short interval nested inside a long one can hide the boundary from LAG. The next interval can overlap the long one while starting after the short one ends.
breaks: Compare each start with the maximum end over all preceding rows in its account, excluding the current row.
contrast: LAG suffices when the ordered end points never decrease.
details:
For account 1, ordered intervals [0,10], [2,3], [4,5], [12,13] give prior ends NULL,10,3,5. The AI starts a new group at 4, returning [0,10], [4,5], [12,13]. The required result is [0,10], [12,13]. Prior maxima NULL,10,10,10 produce it.

[Reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html)
why: LAG loses earlier intervals that extend beyond the immediately preceding end.
bug: LAG loses earlier intervals that extend beyond the immediately preceding end.
flaws: LAG forgets longer intervals before the previous row.
Touching endpoints must always form separate groups.
The final MAX must instead sum all interval lengths.
The window SUM must partition by each interval ID.

title: Required feature coverage
prompt: In PostgreSQL, return each account that has used every feature in required_features. A feature not in that table is irrelevant; usage events may repeat. An account qualifies when no required feature is missing. Judge the query, including when the requirement table is empty.
ai:
SELECT a.account_id
FROM accounts a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM required_features r
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM usage_events u
    WHERE u.account_id = a.account_id
      AND u.feature = r.feature
  )
)
ORDER BY a.account_id;
model: Look for one unmet requirement; accept only accounts for which you cannot find one.
mech: The inner NOT EXISTS identifies a missing feature for an account. The outer NOT EXISTS rejects accounts with any such feature.
breaks: All feature and account keys are non-null. If the requirement table is empty, every account qualifies under the stated rule.
contrast: A raw event count can mistake repeated use of one feature for coverage of several features.
details:
Account 1 covers a and b; account 2 lacks b; account 3 lacks both. Output: account 1. Duplicate events cannot change existence. Removing all requirements makes the outer subquery empty for every account, so output becomes 1,2,3.

[Reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html)
why: The inner NOT EXISTS identifies a missing feature for an account. The outer NOT EXISTS rejects accounts with any such feature.

required_features(feature TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL): (a), (b)
usage_events(account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, feature TEXT NOT NULL):
(1,a), (1,a), (1,b), (2,a), (3,c)

title: Reachable service IDs
prompt: In PostgreSQL, edges is a finite directed graph with non-null integer source and destination IDs. Cycles and duplicate edges are allowed. Return each node reachable from node 1, including node 1 via a zero-edge path. Judge both correctness and termination.
ai:
WITH RECURSIVE reachable(node) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION
  SELECT e.dst
  FROM reachable r
  JOIN edges e ON e.src = r.node
)
SELECT node FROM reachable ORDER BY node;
model: Keep a set of discovered nodes; stop when following edges discovers no new node.
mech: UNION removes duplicate node rows both within a recursive step and against prior results. A finite graph eventually has no undiscovered reachable nodes.
breaks: This relies on the recursive row containing only the node. Adding a changing depth column would make revisits distinct rows.
contrast: UNION ALL would keep generating rows on the 2-to-3-to-2 cycle in this graph.
details:
The seed is {1}; successive new frontiers are {2}, {3}, {4}, then empty. Output: 1,2,3,4. The disconnected self-loop at 5 adds nothing. Each reachable node can enter the result only once.

[Reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html)
why: UNION removes duplicate node rows both within a recursive step and against prior results. A finite graph eventually has no undiscovered reachable nodes.

title: A random arrival at a shuttle stop
prompt: A shuttle repeats this exact schedule forever: a 2-minute gap, then an 18-minute gap, then repeat. A passenger arrives independently at a time uniform over one complete 20-minute cycle. What is the expected time until the next shuttle? Ignore boarding time.
ai: The average gap is (2 + 18)/2 = 10 minutes. An independent passenger lands uniformly within a gap, so the average remaining wait is half of that: 5 minutes.
fix: Weight each gap by its share of clock time: E[wait] = (2^2 + 18^2)/(2*(2+18)) = 8.2 minutes.
model: Long gaps occupy more of the clock, so a random arrival encounters them more often.
mech: Arrival falls in the 2-minute gap with probability 2/20 and in the 18-minute gap with probability 18/20. Conditional mean waits are 1 and 9 minutes.
breaks: Uniform time sampling does not sample the two gap types equally.
contrast: A constant 10-minute gap would give the claimed 5-minute expected wait.
details:
E[wait] = (2/20)(2/2) + (18/20)(18/2) = 8.2 minutes. Independently, the areas under the two residual-wait triangles are 2^2/2 and 18^2/2; dividing their total by 20 gives 8.2.

[Reference](https://www.stat.uchicago.edu/~yibi/teaching/stat317/2021/Lectures/Lecture18.pdf)
why: The calculation gives equal weight to gaps rather than to arrival times.
bug: The calculation gives equal weight to gaps rather than to arrival times.
flaws: A random arrival weights each gap by its duration.
An independent arrival must wait one complete gap.
The two possible gap lengths should be multiplied.
The remaining wait is exponential within a gap.

title: A permutation audit
prompt: Six labeled items are placed into six labeled slots using a uniformly random permutation. Let X count items in their matching slot. An audit retains only permutations with X >= 2. What is E[X | X >= 2]?
ai: It is 456/191, about 2.387. Across all 720 permutations, the sum of X is 720. There are 265 permutations with X = 0 and 264 with X = 1. Removing those leaves 191 permutations whose X values sum to 456.
model: Conditioning changes both the number of eligible cases and the total you average over.
mech: Each item is fixed in 120 permutations, so the total fixed-item count is 6*120 = 720. Removing exactly-one cases subtracts 264 from that total.
breaks: The retained permutations remain equally likely because the original permutation is uniform and retention is deterministic.
contrast: The unconditional expectation is 1; it does not stay 1 after retaining only outcomes with at least two matches.
details:
Inclusion-exclusion gives D5 = 120-120+60-20+5-1 = 44 and D6 = 720-720+360-120+30-6+1 = 265. Exactly one fixed point has 6*D5 = 264 cases. Thus P(X>=2)=191/720 and E[X 1{X>=2}]=456/720. Their ratio is 456/191. Exhaustive enumeration checks all 720 cases.

[Reference](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-226-probabilistic-methods-in-combinatorics-fall-2022/mit18_226_f22_lec03-04.pdf)
why: Each item is fixed in 120 permutations, so the total fixed-item count is 6*120 = 720. Removing exactly-one cases subtracts 264 from that total.

title: A prespecified equivalence decision
prompt: A fixed-horizon randomized experiment prespecifies a single equivalence claim: treatment minus control is strictly between -1.0 and +1.0 percentage points. Use two one-sided normal tests (TOST) with overall alpha 0.05 and a known SE. The estimate is +0.20 percentage points and SE is 0.45 percentage points. No other tests or selection are involved. Does it establish equivalence?
ai: No. Since there are two one-sided tests, each must use alpha 0.025 to keep overall alpha at 0.05. Equivalently, the 95% interval is approximately [-0.682, 1.082], which crosses the upper equivalence margin.
fix: Use alpha 0.05 for each one-sided test. Both pass, so equivalence is established by the prespecified procedure.
model: Equivalence requires passing both boundaries; a false claim must pass the test of a boundary that is actually violated.
mech: This is an intersection-union test. Each one-sided test can use alpha 0.05; rejecting both controls the overall error at 0.05 without dividing alpha by two.
breaks: The margin and testing rule were fixed in advance. This calculation uses the stated known-SE normal model.
contrast: A 95% interval entirely within the margins would also suffice, but is unnecessarily conservative for the specified TOST.
details:
The lower-bound statistic is (0.20+1)/0.45 = 2.6667; the upper-bound statistic is (1-0.20)/0.45 = 1.7778. Both exceed z(0.95)=1.64485. The 90% interval is 0.20 +/- 1.64485*0.45 = [-0.5402,0.9402], strictly inside (-1,1). The one-sided p-values are approximately 0.00383 and 0.03772, so both pass 0.05.

[Reference](https://www.fda.gov/media/71336/download)
why: TOST requires both tests to reject, so splitting alpha in half is unnecessary.
bug: TOST requires both tests to reject, so splitting alpha in half is unnecessary.
flaws: Requiring both rejections needs no alpha split.
The two one-sided p-values must be added first.
The margin must be measured in relative lift.
Known standard errors require a Student t test.
